subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If A, B, C are three independent events such that P(A ∩ Bᶜ ∩ Cᶜ) = 1/4, P(Aᶜ ∩ B ∩ Cᶜ) = 1/8, P(Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ ∩ Cᶜ) = 1/4, then find P(A), P(B) and P(C).

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.61 — SAQ chapter 10 Probability, answer 87 (PDF p.62: on the Probability pages the scan reads book = PDF − 1, not the − 2 that docs/IPE_MATHS_2A_SOURCE.md assumes). Printed appearances: TS 15 · AP 16 (the answer runs from the foot of book p.61 onto the top of p.62). ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed on any Probability SAQ page (book pp.59–62). Three values are asked and one set-up is needed: 1 for the three product equations and 1 for each value found, in the book's order (A, then B, then C). The book's SAQ chapter header carries ★★ and reads '4 + 4 = 8 Marks'; that ★★ is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's, and the 4 + 4 is because Probability holds TWO Section-B slots. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-2A Section B runs Q11–Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q16 and Q17 are the two Probability slots. This question is Q17 of Model Paper 5 (book p.119); it is not in the Bullet Model Paper. No two-book check and no board back-test exist for this paper (no second Maths-2A source in the corpus; answer-book/papers/ holds first-year physics only) — recorded, not hidden. Answers checked: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/3, P(C) = 1/4; back-substitution (1/2)(2/3)(3/4) = 1/4, (1/2)(1/3)(3/4) = 1/8, (1/2)(2/3)(3/4) = 1/4 — agree with the book.

recall_prompt: Say how you would find P(A), P(B), P(C) — how independence turns each given probability into a product, which pairs of equations are divided, and the three values.
insider_note: Dividing two equations that share two factors leaves P(X)/P(Xᶜ), and P(X)/(1 − P(X)) = k is a one-line solve. The third value comes from substituting the first two, not from another division.

steps.label: Independence: write products
steps.margin_note: First mark. Independent events (and their complements) multiply. Number the three equations — the next steps refer to them.

lines.text: A, B, C are independent, so each intersection

recall.must_convey: That by independence each given intersection probability is a product of three factors: (1) P(A)P(Bᶜ)P(Cᶜ) = 1/4, (2) P(Aᶜ)P(B)P(Cᶜ) = 1/8, (3) P(Aᶜ)P(Bᶜ)P(Cᶜ) = 1/4.
accept: independent so each intersection is a product, write the three products equal to a quarter an eighth and a quarter
P A times P B complement times P C complement is one by four and so on for the other two
turn the three given probabilities into products of three factors
independent kabatti prathi intersection product ga rayali, three equations

steps.why: Independence of A, B, C extends to their complements, which is what allows every intersection given to become a product and the unknowns to separate.
common_mistakes: Writing the complements as 1 − P(A ∩ B ∩ C) or similar instead of products of complements.
Not numbering the equations, then being unable to say which are divided.

steps.label: (1) ÷ (3): P(A) = 1/2
steps.margin_note: Second mark. (1) and (3) share P(Bᶜ)P(Cᶜ); dividing leaves P(A)/P(Aᶜ) = 1, so P(A) = 1 − P(A).

recall.must_convey: That dividing (1) by (3) gives P(A)/P(Aᶜ) = 1, so P(A) = 1 − P(A) and P(A) = 1/2.
accept: divide equation one by equation three to get P A over P A complement equals one so P A is half
the common factors cancel leaving P A equals one minus P A, so half
P A by one minus P A is one hence P A is one by two
one ni three tho divide cheste P A by P A complement one, P A half

steps.why: Two equations that differ in only one factor divide to that factor's ratio, and P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A) turns the ratio into an equation in P(A) alone.
common_mistakes: Dividing (1) by (2), which leaves two unknowns.

steps.label: (2) ÷ (3): P(B) = 1/3
steps.margin_note: Third mark. (2) and (3) share P(Aᶜ)P(Cᶜ); dividing gives P(B)/P(Bᶜ) = 1/2.

recall.must_convey: That dividing (2) by (3) gives P(B)/P(Bᶜ) = 1/2, so 2P(B) = 1 − P(B) and P(B) = 1/3.
accept: divide equation two by three to get P B over P B complement equals half so P B is a third
two P B equals one minus P B gives one by three
the ratio is one eighth over one quarter which is half, so P B is one third
two ni three tho divide cheste P B by P B complement half, P B one by three

steps.why: The same move as for P(A), with the ratio 1/2 instead of 1.
common_mistakes: Inverting the ratio and getting P(B) = 2/3.

steps.label: From (3): P(C) = 1/4
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Put P(Aᶜ) = 1/2 and P(Bᶜ) = 2/3 into (3): (1/3)·P(Cᶜ) = 1/4, so P(Cᶜ) = 3/4.

recall.must_convey: That substituting P(Aᶜ) = 1/2 and P(Bᶜ) = 2/3 into (3) gives P(Cᶜ) = 3/4, so P(C) = 1/4; the three answers are 1/2, 1/3, 1/4.
accept: substitute half and two thirds into equation three to get P C complement three quarters so P C is a quarter
a third times P C complement is a quarter so P C complement is three by four and P C is one by four
the answers are half, a third and a quarter
equation three lo pettithe P C complement 3 by 4, P C 1 by 4

steps.why: With two values known, the third equation has one unknown left. The complement is found first because that is what the equation contains.
common_mistakes: Substituting P(A) = 1/2 and P(B) = 1/3 instead of their complements into (3).
